Without A, filtering 'Dragons' would miss tags stored as 'Dragons'. But that makes them compatible, not conflicting, and legacy mixed-case rows are an edge case beyond this scenario.

rows.explanation: B adds a 60s in-memory cache for GET /api/tags, invalidated only when articles are created. A makes article deletion also delete orphaned tags. After merge, deleting an article removes tags from the DB but never invalidates B's cache, so GET /api/tags keeps returning the deleted tags for up to 60s. A's integration test checks the DB directly, so it passes, but the API behavior is stale (e.g. create article with tag 'solo', GET tags (cached), delete article, GET tags still lists 'solo'). B's cache correctness relies on tags only changing via creation, which A's change breaks.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: After merge, userChangePassword hashes newPassword and passes it to userUpdatePrisma, which (from A) now hashes any password again. The stored value becomes bcrypt(bcrypt(newPassword)), so the user can never log in with the new password after using POST /api/user/password. B's own test only checks the stored value differs from plain text and the old hash, so it still passes. Separately, A's fix for PUT /api/user fixes the same plain-text storage problem at the DB layer that B solves by hashing in the controller, so the hashing is duplicated.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: A makes Article.updatedAt auto-update via @updatedAt and removes the manual updatedAt set in articleUpdatePrisma. B adds a views counter on Article, incremented via prisma.article.update on every article GET. With @updatedAt in the merged schema, Prisma sets updatedAt on every update call, including B's view-increment, so every read of an article bumps its updatedAt. Before A, B's increment did not touch updatedAt (it was only set manually in articleUpdatePrisma). Merged, the article's updatedAt reflects the last view rather than the last edit, and articleViewer exposes updatedAt to API clients. Neither change alone causes this: A alone only has real edits updating the timestamp, and B alone leaves updatedAt untouched on reads.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Both changes solve the same problem, that tags no longer attached to any article should not appear in the tag list, in two different ways. A physically deletes orphaned tags when an article is deleted, and B filters unused tags out of the tag list at read time. Each alone makes the same integration test pass (the two tests are essentially identical). Merged, the code is redundant: either the delete-time cleanup or the read-time filter should be removed. Behavior is not wrong, but the intent is duplicated.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Both changes fix the same bug (the feed returning articles from all authors, not just followed ones). A filters in the database query (where author.followedBy), while B filters in the controller after fetching with limit/offset. Merged, the same filtering is done twice: once in the query and once in memory. The second filter is redundant (a no-op) and one of the two should be removed. Both also make identical edits to articles.int.test.ts and add two near-duplicate new tests. Note that B's post-filter on a paginated unfiltered query would have been buggy alone (pages could come back short), whereas with A's query filter it is harmless, but the intent duplication remains.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Both changes add the same author-only check to DELETE /api/articles/:slug. A puts it inline in the articlesDelete controller. B adds a requireArticleAuthor middleware and wires it into the delete route. Merged, the route runs the middleware first (403 for non-authors), then the controller repeats the same user lookup, article lookup and 403 check. The second check can never fire after the first passes, so the ownership logic exists twice and costs an extra pair of DB queries per delete. Both changes also remove the same 'known bug' test and add near-identical new tests. Behavior is still correct, but this is the same problem solved in two ways, and one of them should be dropped.

rows.label: no_conflict
rows.explanation: Change A truncates slugs to 100 characters inside slugfy, so long titles no longer produce overly long slugs. Change B caps titles at 150 characters in the create validator. These are different layers: one bounds the slug output, the other bounds the input title. A title of 100-150 characters is accepted by B and yields a truncated slug under A; this is correct and consistent. Titles over 150 are rejected before slugging. One could argue both address the 'too-long title/slug' problem, but they constrain different values (title vs. slug) and neither makes the other redundant. Slug uniqueness is not newly threatened beyond what A alone introduces, and B's limit does not interact with it. No runtime breakage or duplicated work is apparent.

rows.label: no_conflict
rows.explanation: Change A adds database indexes on Article.authorUsername and Article.updatedAt, which are performance-only and do not change query semantics. Change B adds a sort query parameter ('created' or 'updated') to the article list endpoint. The two are complementary: A's updatedAt index supports B's default ordering, and neither breaks assumptions the other relies on. They do not solve the same problem in different ways. B's sort=created ordering does not benefit from an index, but that is a performance gap, not a correctness or duplication conflict.

rows.label: no_conflict
rows.explanation: Change A caches the tag list and invalidates it via a prisma.$use middleware on writes to Tag or Article models. Change B adds a prisma.tag.deleteMany after article deletion to clean orphan tags. In the merged code, article.delete triggers the middleware (model Article, action delete) and clears the cache, but the subsequent tag.deleteMany runs after that invalidation. Between the two calls, a concurrent getTags request could repopulate the cache with the orphan tags still present. The later tag.deleteMany also triggers the middleware (model Tag, action deleteMany), which clears the cache again, so any stale cache is invalidated after the orphan cleanup. The cache is therefore correct in the merged code. Single-sequence behavior is also fine: both writes invalidate the cache. A's invalidation is model-based and covers B's new write, so the two changes compose correctly.

rows.label: no_conflict
rows.explanation: Both changes address the plain-text password storage problem. Change A fixes the known bug in PUT /api/user by hashing the password inside userUpdatePrisma. Change B adds a separate POST /api/user/password endpoint with its own DB helper that hashes the new password. B's endpoint doesn't pass through userUpdatePrisma, so there's no double hashing at runtime, and both paths store correct hashes. However, the intent overlaps: after A, PUT /api/user already supports changing the password (and A's test asserts it works for login), while B introduces a second, parallel way to change the password (with current-password verification) and a duplicate DB write helper. The merged code has two different mechanisms for the same job, and one should be removed or the PUT path should stop accepting passwords.

rows.label: no_conflict
rows.explanation: Change A renames the JWT_SECRET env var to AUTH_JWT_SECRET across code, tests, README and .env.test. Change B adds a password reset token module that uses a separate RESET_TOKEN_SECRET and adds that var to .env.test. The two .env.test edits touch adjacent lines but merge cleanly, giving AUTH_JWT_SECRET, NODE_ENV, and RESET_TOKEN_SECRET, which is correct. B's code never reads JWT_SECRET or AUTH_JWT_SECRET, so the rename does not affect it. B's tests use only RESET_TOKEN_SECRET. There is no runtime or intent conflict.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Both changes define the default page size for GET /api/articles and set it to different values. A lowers the default limit in articlesListPrisma from 20 to 10, and its test asserts that a plain GET /api/articles returns 10 articles. B adds ?page=N, whose pages are PAGE_SIZE = 20 articles each, and its test asserts that page=1 returns 20 of 25 articles. In the merged code, no-parameter requests return 10 per page while ?page=N returns 20 per page, so the same endpoint has two inconsistent page sizes. A client that pages with ?page=N gets pages of 20. A client that omits ?page gets 10. Page 1 of ?page is not the same as the default response. B's constant duplicates the default limit that A is changing, so one definition should be removed. Both tests pass independently because the page path always sets limit explicitly, but the page size is defined in two places and they now disagree.

rows.label: no_conflict
rows.explanation: Change A adds a log line after successful article creation; Change B adds an early-return validation rejecting more than 10 tags before any creation. They are orthogonal: the validation returns before the log line, so rejected requests are not logged as created, which is correct. Accepted requests still log. Both sets of tests remain valid (A's test uses no tags; B's tests don't depend on logging). No concrete failure scenario or duplicated purpose.

rows.label: no_conflict
rows.explanation: Change A refactors the where-clause construction in articlesListPrisma with equivalent semantics (undefined fields were ignored by Prisma before; now they are simply not set). The one subtle difference is that empty-string values are now falsy and skipped for authorUsername, whereas before an empty string would filter on ''. Change B calls articlesListPrisma with a username from req.params, which is always non-empty for the route. Passing undefined for limit and offset triggers the default parameters, so behavior is unchanged. There is no duplication of intent: A is an internal refactor and B adds a new endpoint reusing the function. The two work correctly together.

rows.label: no_conflict
rows.explanation: The two changes add unrelated count endpoints: one counts comments per article (GET /api/articles/:slug/comments/count), the other counts articles per tag (GET /api/tags/:tag/count). They live in different routers and controllers, use distinct URL paths, and each reads the article table only for its own purpose (existence check vs. tag-filtered count). There is no shared state, no overlapping route, and no duplicated purpose, so the merged code behaves correctly.

rows.label: no_conflict
rows.explanation: Change A only adds JSDoc comments to userUpdatePrisma and an interface comment; it makes no behavioral change. Change B adds trimming of bio and image inside the function plus an integration test. The merged result keeps B's trimming and A's docs. The JSDoc says 'Fields left out are kept' and B's code sets bio/image to undefined when absent, which Prisma ignores, so that remains true. The docs don't mention trimming, but this is not a behavioral or intent conflict.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Change A soft-deletes articles (sets deletedAt, hides them from get/list/feed queries). Change B adds a /tags/counts endpoint that counts articles per tag via prisma.tag _count of article, which does not filter on deletedAt. After merge, soft-deleted articles remain in the DB with their tag relations intact, so getTagCounts will still count deleted articles. Scenario: alice creates an article tagged 'x' and deletes it; /api/tags/counts still returns {tag:'x', count:1} even though no visible article uses it. The filter `count > 0` in B was meant to hide unused tags, but the soft-delete breaks that assumption. Neither change alone has this bug (before A, hard delete removed the relation row).

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Both changes solve the same problem: making email handling case- and whitespace-insensitive. Change A normalizes the email in the login and register controllers through a new normalizeEmail util. Change B normalizes it inside userCreatePrisma and userGetEmailPrisma with inline trim().toLowerCase(). In the merged code every email is normalized twice (controller, then DB helper). The double normalization is idempotent and harmless at runtime, but the two changes implement the same fix in two different places and ways, so one of them should be removed. Each side also adds an integration test that asserts essentially the same behavior.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Change A makes the article slug change when the title is renamed, so the slug (Article's primary key) can now be mutated. Change B adds a RecentView table that stores article slugs as plain strings, with no foreign key to Article. After a rename, the old slug stays in RecentView, so recentArticlesPrisma silently drops the renamed article via the flatMap (bySlug.get(oldSlug) is undefined). The user's recent list loses the article even though they viewed it, and stale rows pile up and take up KEEP slots. Neither change breaks alone: before A, slugs never changed, and B alone is consistent. B's slug-keyed storage assumes slugs are immutable, which A violates. Once the old slug is freed, a new article with that slug could also show up in recents as if it had been viewed.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Change A switches the list ordering in articlesListPrisma from updatedAt desc to createdAt desc. Change B adds an ?after=<slug> cursor that filters with updatedAt < cursor.updatedAt, assuming the list is ordered by updatedAt desc. In the merged code the filter uses updatedAt while the ordering uses createdAt, so the cursor no longer matches the sort order. Concrete scenario: articles One, Two and Three are created in that order, then One is edited so its updatedAt is the latest. The list ordered by createdAt gives three, two, one. Requesting ?limit=2&after=two filters updatedAt < two.updatedAt, which excludes One because its updatedAt is newest, so the page after 'two' is empty and article 'one' is never reached. Pagination silently drops items. B's new test sets only updatedAt (leaving createdAt at creation order) and still passes only because creation order happens to match.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Change A adds a rule to the PUT /api/user validator that rejects non-https image URLs, so users can no longer set a plain-http image through that endpoint. Change B adds a new PUT /api/user/image route that sets the same field but skips userUpdateValidator, accepting any string, including http:// URLs or arbitrary text. In the merged code, the https-only rule can be bypassed through the new endpoint, so the invariant A introduces is not enforced. A concrete scenario is PUT /api/user/image with {image: "http://x/a.png"}, which returns 200 and stores the http URL, while the same value sent to PUT /api/user returns 400. The two changes are not duplicates; B was written without knowing about A's rule, but the combination produces inconsistent validation of the same field.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Both changes add a way to list the current authenticated user's favorited articles: A adds a new GET /api/user/favorites endpoint, B adds a ?favorited=me shortcut on GET /api/articles. Both end up calling articlesListPrisma with the current user's username as the favorited filter and render the result with articleViewer, and each ships an integration test asserting the same scenario (bob favorites 'liked', list returns only 'liked', 401 without a token). Nothing breaks at runtime, but the merged code gives two different APIs for the same feature, so one should be dropped.
